topics.label: Introduction and lecture objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture within the cancer course and sets out its learning objectives.

topics.label: Cancer evolution and the origins of genetic susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how mutations arising in susceptible cells can support clonal evolution towards cancer within a permissive microenvironment.

topics.label: Environmental cancer risks and the bad-luck debate
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine the contribution of environmental exposures to cancer risk despite uncertainty and variation in who develops cancer.

topics.label: Infectious agents in cancer development
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infections can drive cancer, with Burkitt lymphoma illustrating the cooperation between infectious agents and cellular mutations.

topics.label: Mechanisms of DNA damage from environmental carcinogens
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how environmental exposures produce DNA damage and mutations through processes whose effects depend on their interaction with cellular metabolism and repair.

topics.label: Tumour initiation and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics distinguish mutation-initiating activity from the promotion of tumour growth and explain why initiated cells may require additional growth-supporting conditions.

topics.label: Developmental and tissue susceptibility, with a recap of carcinogenic mechanisms
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics complete the account of carcinogenic mechanisms by explaining context-dependent susceptibility and then recapping the mechanisms already introduced.

topics.label: Methods and evidence for assessing cancer causation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how evidence can link exposures to cancer and why the biological systems used to obtain that evidence limit the conclusions.

topics.label: Concluding summary and risk–benefit decisions
topics.groupedBecause: This closing draws together the lecture's conclusions about environmental cancer risks and their assessment through the lens of everyday risk–benefit decisions.
